newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane Danny causes little damage to U.S. crops.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Danny causes little damage to U.S. crops.

text.p: Most crops in the southeast United States escaped damage from the remnants of Hurricane Danny which drifted up the Alabama/Mississippi border early this week, crop experts said.
Two counties in Alabama were hit by heavy downpours last week which caused crop damage, but agricultural production in Mississippi, Louisiana and Georgia was unharmed.
"Remnants from Hurricane Danny washed away tons of top soil in Baldwin and Mobile (counties)," said Jack Thompson, commissioner of Agriculture and Industry of Alabama.

Hurricane Danny slammed into Mobile, Alabama on July 19, bringing heavy rains of up to 10 to 20 inches before being downgraded to a tropical storm later in the day, Weather Services Corp meteorologist Mike Palmerino said.
But Palmerino noted "the remains of Danny may redevelop off the North Carolina/Virginia coast later Thursday."
It was still too early to assess the damage in Alabama.

"It's going to be two to three weeks before we can give specific economic losses for Mobile county," said Andrew Greer, county agent, Mobile County. He said cotton, corn, soybeans, fruits and vegetables received some damage.
Ed Tunnell, extension coordinator for Baldwin County, Alabama, said cotton, soybeans and corn were affected by Danny.
"We have over 50,000 to 60,000 acres of soybeans (and) all of them were damaged to some extent, basically from water standing in fields and high winds," Tunnell told Reuters.
"For three days last week it (Danny) pumped water on us. The corn crop was made. We would have started harvesting this week but most of that corn was blown down," Tunnell said.
Farmers plan on harvesting the corn as soon as it dries out, he said, adding yield losses were difficult to assess.
Baldwin has about 10,000 acres of corn and about 14,000 acres of cotton. Some cotton was damaged but Tunnell said Baldwin would be able to produce a fairly good cotton crop.
Elsewhere in the Southeast crop damage was very limited.

"Mississippi did get significant rainfall from Hurricane Danny but not enough to hurt agricultural operations or crops in the counties of Jackson, George and Harrison," Mississippi Agricultural Statistics Service statistician Thomas Gregory said.
Louisiana did not receive much damage. "I have not heard of any reports of significant damage," said Ron Harrell, commodity director, Louisiana Farm Bureau, Baton Rouge.
"There is no crop damage in Georgia and in fact we are hoping for more rain in southern Georgia," said Tommy Irvin, Georgia Commissioner of Agriculture.
